title: C# Login Project · Code a Hash Table
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: Choose the model answer: A five-bucket hash table uses h(k) = k MOD 5 with linear probing. Insert keys 7, 12 and 17 in that order into an empty table. State each final index.
questions.answer: 7 hashes to 2 and is stored at 2. 12 also hashes to 2, so probes to 3. 17 also hashes to 2; 2 and 3 are occupied, so it goes to 4.

blocks.title: The problem: more than one user
blocks.text: A single username comparison is not scalable. We need a way to store and find many usernames.

blocks.title: What is a hash function?
blocks.text: Convert the username to a number, then use % tableSize to choose a bucket index. Our small function is deliberately simple for learning.

blocks.title: What if two names choose one bucket?
blocks.text: That is a collision. Use linear probing: try the next bucket, wrapping to the beginning when necessary.

blocks.title: Lookups must use the same rule
blocks.text: Recalculate the starting bucket from the username, then probe through occupied buckets until the username or an empty bucket is found.

blocks.title: Worked example · Build a real hash-table index
blocks.text: Create the bucket array manually: the hash function is visible, not hidden inside Dictionary.

blocks.title: Insert with linear probing
blocks.text: int index = Hash(username, SIZE); while (usernames[index] != null) { index = (index + 1) % SIZE; } usernames[index] = username;
